Basilius Besler, HORTUS EYSTETTENSIS (1613), Ordo Autumnalis.
Two tomato plates, transcribed from the engraved captions on the plates
themselves. Both readings were verified against the plate images held in this
directory, at full resolution, on 2026-09-03.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
BILDTAFEL 319 — Classis Autumnalis, Fol. 1 — KU 2894 vol. 3 p. [194]
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Engraved caption, three plants on one plate, left to right as printed:

II. Melo Saccharinus variegatus
I Poma amoris fructu luteo.
III. Pseudocolocynthis Pomiformis.

The tomato is number I, the centre plant: a branching plant with pinnate,
irregularly lobed leaves, star-shaped pale flowers, and pale yellow to cream
fruits that are strongly ribbed and markedly flattened. The two flanking
fruits are a striped sugar melon (II, lower left) and a dark striped gourd
(III, lower right); neither is a tomato and neither should be scored as one.

The 1640 edition of the same plate glosses the Latin in German:

1. Poma Amoris fructu luteo. — Lieboepffel oder Goldoepffel.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
BILDTAFEL 320 — Classis Autumnalis, Fol. 2 — KU 2894 vol. 3 p. [197]
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Engraved caption, bottom centre, the whole plate being one plant:

Poma amoris fructu rubro.

A single tomato plant occupying the full plate: pinnate lobed leaves,
star-shaped pale flowers, and eight or more large fruits, deep red, heavily
ribbed and strongly flattened, with several smaller green and brown unripe
fruits. The artist's monogram is engraved at the base of the stem.

The 1640 edition of the same plate glosses the Latin in German:

1. Poma Amoris fructu rubro. — Rothe Goldoepffel / Lieboepffel.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
WHY THESE TWO PLATES MATTER HERE
--------------------------------------------------------------------

They give the corpus a dated, named, coloured depiction of the tomato from
1613, in a work whose author died in 1629, showing the two fruit colours as
separate named kinds — luteo and rubro, yellow and red — and showing both as
strongly ribbed and flattened. That is directly on the fruit-shape argument,
and it is the holder's own printed caption doing the naming, not a modern
identification.

The German gloss is evidence in its own right: Lieboepffel and Goldoepffel
are the German counterparts of the Italian pomodoro and the Latin mala aurea
and poma amoris that this corpus already tracks, and they are attached here to
a specific plant in a specific year.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
BESLER'S OWN PRINTED INDEX TO THE CLASSIS AUTUMNALIS
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Read 2026-09-03 from the letterpress description sheet that accompanies the
autumn plates (1640 edition, BHL 45339 page [339], "Classis Autumnalis,
description 1-33"). Transcribed verbatim, Latin name then Besler's own German
gloss:

Fol. 1.
1. Poma Amoris fructu luteo: Lieboepffel oder Goldoepffel.
2. Melosaccharinus variegatus. Wolriechende Zucker Melonen.
3. Pseudocolocynthis pomiformis.
Falsche Colocynthoepffel / mit
gruenschwartzen Macklen.

Fol. 2.
1. Poma Amoris fructu rubro. Rothe Goldoepffel / Lieboepffel.

Fol. 3.
Melanzana fructu pallido. Gelb Melanzan / Dolloepffel.

Fol. 5.
1. Solanum Pomiferum. Dolloepffel auss Mohrenlandt / oder
Mohrenoepffel.
2. Amaracus vulgaris. Gemeiner Garten-Majoran.

BESLER USES *SOLANUM POMIFERUM*, AND NOT FOR THE TOMATO. It is folio 5, a
different plant from the tomato plates at folios 1 and 2, and he glosses it in
German with the SAME word he gives the aubergine at folio 3 -- Dolloepffel,
mad-apple -- adding that it comes "auss Mohrenlandt", from Moorenland. His
tomatoes are Poma Amoris and are glossed Lieboepffel and Goldoepffel, love-apple
and gold-apple.

So within one printed index Besler separates three things that this corpus has
repeatedly seen conflated: Poma Amoris (the tomato, fols. 1-2), Melanzana (the
aubergine, fol. 3) and Solanum Pomiferum (fol. 5, glossed as an aubergine-type
mad-apple). He is a witness for the DISTINCTION, not for the equation.
